paths.title: From regression to Gaussian processes
paths.summary: Start from least squares and end at the kernel view of learning: regularized linear models, margins, Bayesian kernel regression, and the infinite-width bridge to neural networks.
paths.audience: Newcomers with undergraduate calculus and linear algebra; no machine-learning background assumed.

steps.objective: Derive the ridge estimate w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy, explain how λ trades bias for variance, and show that it equals the posterior mean under Gaussian noise and a Gaussian prior on w.
steps.why: Least squares is the simplest learner whose every quantity can be computed by hand; everything later on this path generalizes it.

steps.objective: Fit a logistic regression by maximizing the Bernoulli log-likelihood, interpret a coefficient as a change in log-odds, and add an L2 penalty to it.
steps.why: The atlas edge says linear and generalized linear methods share explicit features and regularization while using different response distributions: same linear predictor, new likelihood.

steps.objective: State the soft-margin SVM objective (hinge loss plus ‖w‖² penalty), explain why only support vectors determine the solution, and use the kernel trick to classify with an RBF kernel.
steps.why: SVMs swap the logistic loss for the hinge loss and introduce kernels, the key idea needed for Gaussian processes. There is no direct atlas edge from logistic regression; the step is a change of loss function.

steps.objective: Compute a GP posterior mean and variance for a small 1-D dataset with a squared-exponential kernel, and show that with a linear kernel the posterior mean equals the ridge prediction.
steps.why: The atlas edge describes a shared kernel regularization framework with different loss functions and uncertainty interpretation; the GP adds calibrated predictive variance that the SVM lacks (and the ridge↔GP edge is an exact conditional identity).

steps.objective: Explain the two infinite-width limits: a randomly initialized wide network is a GP (NNGP), and gradient-descent training of it behaves like kernel regression with the neural tangent kernel.
steps.why: The atlas edge: infinite-width initialization connects neural networks to GPs, while training uses a tangent kernel. This is the doorway from classical kernels to learning-dynamics theory.

paths.title: Signals to convolutional networks
paths.summary: Learn how sampled signals are represented in frequency and scale, how fixed filters are built, and how designed wavelet filter banks become the scattering transform and then learned CNNs.
paths.audience: Newcomers with undergraduate calculus (complex exponentials help); no signal-processing course required.

steps.objective: State the sampling theorem (sample faster than twice the highest frequency), predict the alias frequency of an undersampled sinusoid, and explain why an anti-aliasing filter comes before the sampler.
steps.why: Every digital signal starts as samples; knowing what sampling destroys is the first condition for any later estimate or model.

steps.objective: Compute a DFT with numpy.fft, read a magnitude spectrum, and explain the time–frequency trade-off of a finite window.
steps.why: The atlas edge is an exact conditional identity: uniform sampling replicates spectra, and non-overlap under a band limit enables ideal reconstruction. Aliasing is only fully understood in the frequency domain.

steps.objective: Implement a moving-average and a simple FIR low-pass filter, and verify numerically that convolution in time equals multiplication of spectra.
steps.why: The atlas edge: Fourier representations and FFT computation support filtering and convolution. The convolution theorem turns filter design into spectrum shaping.

steps.objective: Run a two-level Haar wavelet decomposition, identify approximation and detail coefficients, and explain why wavelets localize in both time and scale where Fourier bases do not.
steps.why: The atlas edge: filter-bank operations construct multiresolution approximations and detail coefficients. Wavelets are cascades of the filters you just built.

steps.objective: Describe the scattering transform as cascaded wavelet convolution, complex modulus and averaging, and state which invariances (translation, small deformations) it is designed to provide.
steps.why: The atlas edge: wavelet convolutions, modulus and averaging construct scattering representations — a convolutional network whose filters are designed rather than learned.

steps.objective: Train a small CNN on an image dataset, compute the output shape and parameter count of a conv layer, and contrast its learned filters with the fixed scattering filters.
steps.why: The atlas edge: scattering gives a mathematically structured convolutional representation, not a universal identity with trained CNNs. Comparing the two shows what learning adds and what structure guarantees.

paths.title: Estimation to control: Kalman → LQG → MPC
paths.summary: Turn regression into recursive state estimation, learn what makes states observable and reachable, and compose estimators with optimal feedback into LQG and model predictive control.
paths.audience: Learners comfortable with linear algebra and Gaussian probability, e.g. after a first ML or signals course.

steps.objective: Write the regularized least-squares estimate and interpret the regularizer as a Gaussian prior on the weights.
steps.why: Least squares with a prior is the static special case of the Kalman filter.

steps.objective: Implement the Kalman predict/update equations for a constant-velocity tracker, and explain the gain as a ratio of prior to measurement uncertainty.
steps.why: The atlas edge: regression weights can be treated as a state for sequential Gaussian inference — recursive least squares is a Kalman filter with a static state.

steps.objective: Compute the Fisher information of a linear-Gaussian measurement model and relate its inverse to the Cramér–Rao lower bound on estimator variance.
steps.why: The atlas edge: stochastic estimation must incorporate measurement/process uncertainty and prior information, not only an unweighted fit. The Kalman covariance has an information-form dual.

steps.objective: Test observability of an LTI system with the rank of [C; CA; …; CAⁿ⁻¹] and design a Luenberger observer for a two-state system.
steps.why: The atlas edge is a conditional identity: for known deterministic linear dynamics and independent Gaussian sensor noise, initial-state Fisher information is the (noise-weighted) observability Gramian. Observability asks whether the data can pin down the state at all.

steps.objective: Test reachability with the rank of [B, AB, …, Aⁿ⁻¹B] and state the duality between the pairs (A, B) and (Aᵀ, Bᵀ).
steps.why: The atlas edge is an exact duality: the LTI reachability pair (A,B) is dual to the observability pair (Aᵀ,Bᵀ). Whatever you learned about sensing transfers to actuation.

steps.objective: Solve the discrete algebraic Riccati equation (e.g. with scipy.linalg.solve_discrete_are) to obtain the LQR gain K, and show how changing Q and R trades state error against control effort.
steps.why: The atlas edge: state feedback requires the appropriate reachable or stabilizable structure. LQR is the optimal state feedback once reachability holds.

steps.objective: Build an LQG controller by feeding Kalman-filter estimates into the LQR gain, and state the separation principle and the assumptions it relies on.
steps.why: The atlas edge: LQG combines linear-quadratic feedback with Gaussian state estimation under its model assumptions — the filter from step 2 meets the controller from step 6.

steps.objective: Formulate a finite-horizon constrained quadratic program for a linear plant, apply only the first input each step (receding horizon), and explain when unconstrained MPC with an LQR terminal cost reproduces LQR.
steps.why: MPC keeps the quadratic cost of LQR/LQG but handles input and state constraints by re-solving online. The atlas has no direct LQG–MPC edge; the step is a pedagogical generalization.

steps.objective: Describe a predictive safety filter: given a learner's proposed action, solve a small MPC problem that keeps the system in a safe set and fall back to a certified plan when needed.
steps.why: The atlas edge: a predictive safety filter can modify a learner's proposed input and fall back to a previously certified plan — MPC becomes a guard around learned controllers.

paths.title: Graphical models to belief-state world models
paths.summary: Follow one idea — factorize a joint distribution and pass messages — from static graphical models through HMMs and dynamic Bayesian networks to learned latent world models and belief-state planning.
paths.audience: Learners comfortable with Bayes' rule and conditional independence who want the probabilistic backbone of world models.

steps.objective: Write the joint distribution implied by a small directed and a small undirected graph, and read off one conditional independence from each.
steps.why: Graphical models are the shared language for every factorized model on this path.

steps.objective: Convert a Bayesian network into a factor graph by drawing one factor node per local conditional and connecting it to its variable arguments.
steps.why: The atlas edge: factor graphs explicitly represent local factors and their variable arguments, the form message passing operates on.

steps.objective: Run sum-product by hand on a three-variable chain to obtain exact marginals, and explain why the result is exact only on cycle-free graphs.
steps.why: The atlas edge is a conditional identity: sum-product computes exact marginal functions on a finite cycle-free factor graph.

steps.objective: Implement the forward–backward algorithm for a two-state HMM and use Viterbi to decode the most likely regime sequence.
steps.why: The atlas edge: forward–backward inference is a sum-product instance on a hidden-state chain.

steps.objective: Draw the two-slice template of a dynamic Bayesian network and show how both the HMM and the linear-Gaussian state-space model (Kalman) are special cases.
steps.why: The atlas edge: HMMs are a discrete-state special case of dynamic Bayesian networks. DBNs let states be factored and continuous.

steps.objective: Describe PlaNet/Dreamer-style recurrent state-space models: a deterministic recurrent path plus a stochastic latent, trained with reconstruction and KL terms, used to imagine action-conditioned rollouts.
steps.why: The atlas edge: PlaNet combines deterministic recurrence, stochastic latent state, variational filtering and action-conditioned prediction — a learned DBN with actions.

steps.objective: Write the belief update b′(s′) ∝ O(o | s′) Σₛ T(s′ | s, a) b(s), and explain why planning over beliefs makes a POMDP a fully observed (but continuous-state) MDP.
steps.why: The atlas edge: PlaNet formulates control from pixels as partial-observation planning in a learned latent model. The POMDP is the formal problem the world model approximates.

steps.objective: Define a predictive state as the vector of probabilities of future observation tests given history, and state the result that a finite POMDP has a linear PSR of dimension at most its number of hidden states.
steps.why: The atlas edge: a finite POMDP admits a finite linear predictive-state representation. PSRs replace unobservable latent states with predictions you can check against data.

paths.title: Sequence models: RNNs, state-space models and attention
paths.summary: Start from softmax attention, see how linear attention turns it into a recurrence, then follow recurrent memory through HiPPO, S4 and Mamba until Mamba-2's state-space duality closes the loop back to attention.
paths.audience: Learners who have trained a neural network and know at a high level what an RNN and a transformer are.

steps.objective: Implement scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask, and state its O(T²) time and memory cost in sequence length T.
steps.why: Softmax attention is the reference point every efficient sequence model on this path is measured against.

steps.objective: Replace softmax(QKᵀ)V with a kernel feature map φ(Q)(φ(K)ᵀV), show the cost becomes linear in T, and say what is lost relative to softmax.
steps.why: The atlas edge: kernel-feature attention permits a recurrent formulation; it is not a universal exact softmax rewrite.

steps.objective: Show that causal linear attention is an RNN with a matrix-valued state Sₜ = Sₜ₋₁ + φ(kₜ)vₜᵀ, then write a standard RNN hₜ = σ(W hₜ₋₁ + U xₜ) and explain vanishing/exploding gradients via the eigenvalues of W.
steps.why: The atlas edge is a conditional identity: the specified kernelized causal attention admits recurrent accumulation of summaries.

steps.objective: Explain how HiPPO derives a linear ODE for coefficients that compress the input history onto orthogonal (Legendre) polynomials, giving memory by design rather than by training.
steps.why: The atlas edge: polynomial projection dynamics produce recurrent memory updates — a principled answer to the RNN memory problem.

steps.objective: Show that a discretized linear SSM can be computed either as a recurrence or as a convolution with kernel K = (CB, CAB, CA²B, …), and explain why S4's structured A makes that kernel cheap.
steps.why: The atlas edge: HiPPO supplies structured memory dynamics used in the SSM lineage; S4 initializes its state matrix from HiPPO.

steps.objective: Explain what selectivity means in Mamba (step size and B, C depend on the input), why that breaks the fixed-convolution form, and how a parallel scan keeps training efficient.
steps.why: The atlas edge: input-dependent selectivity extends fixed SSM dynamics and removes fixed-convolution evaluation.

steps.objective: Describe state-space duality: a selective SSM with scalar-times-identity state matrix computes the same map as a semiseparable masked matrix, enabling a quadratic attention-like and a linear recurrent algorithm.
steps.why: The atlas edge: structured state-space duality refines selective SSM computation through semiseparable matrices.

steps.objective: Describe how Griffin (local attention plus gated linear recurrence) and Jamba (Mamba plus attention plus mixture-of-experts layers) interleave mechanisms, and state the recall-versus-constant-memory trade-off that motivates them.
steps.why: Having seen that SSMs and attention are related but not identical, the practical answer is to combine them; the atlas edges cite Griffin (attention–hybrid) and Jamba (Mamba–hybrid). There is no direct SSD–hybrid edge.

paths.title: Physics-informed and operator learning
paths.summary: Learn dynamics from data with sparse regression and Koopman embeddings, then build physics into neural networks through structured vector fields, PDE residuals and operator learning.
paths.audience: Learners with ODE basics and some neural-network experience, e.g. engineers or physicists entering ML.

steps.objective: Solve a least-squares problem Θ ξ ≈ y for coefficients ξ over a matrix Θ of candidate features.
steps.why: Equation discovery on this path is regression over a library of candidate terms.

steps.objective: Recover the Lorenz equations from simulated trajectories with sequentially thresholded least squares over a polynomial library, and explain how SINDYc adds control inputs.
steps.why: The atlas edge: dynamics discovery uses regression over candidate governing terms, with sparsity-promoting selection.

steps.objective: Run DMD on snapshot data to fit a linear operator, and explain how the Koopman operator acts linearly on observables of a nonlinear system and why finite closure is an assumption to test.
steps.why: The atlas edge: the controlled sparse-identification paper explicitly connects to DMD and Koopman operator theory — an alternative to sparse nonlinear terms is linear dynamics in lifted coordinates.

steps.objective: Define a neural ODE dx/dt = f_θ(x, t), integrate it with an ODE solver, and train it on trajectory data by backpropagating through (or adjoint-solving) the solver.
steps.why: Instead of choosing a library or a lifting, learn the vector field itself. There is no direct Koopman–neural-ODE edge; this is a change of representation.

steps.objective: Train a Hamiltonian neural network that learns a scalar H(q, p) and uses (∂H/∂p, −∂H/∂q) as the vector field, and verify that its predicted energy stays nearly constant on a pendulum.
steps.why: The atlas edge: Hamiltonian structure constrains the vector field for conservative dynamics — the neural ODE with physics built in.

steps.objective: Solve a 1-D heat or Burgers equation with a PINN by adding the autodiff PDE residual and boundary terms to the loss, and name one known failure mode (e.g. stiff or multiscale problems).
steps.why: The atlas edge: both incorporate physical knowledge, but structured vector fields and soft PDE residuals are different constructions.

steps.objective: Explain how FNO and DeepONet learn a map from input functions (e.g. initial conditions) to solution functions, and why one trained operator can answer many PDE instances while a PINN solves one.
steps.why: The atlas edge: both address differential-equation problems, but operator learning and residual-constrained single solutions differ.

paths.title: Model-based RL, planning and safe action
paths.summary: From the RL problem to learned world models, receding-horizon planning, and the certificates (safety filters, barrier and Lyapunov functions) that keep learned controllers inside safe sets.
paths.audience: Learners who know basic probability and have seen an MDP; control background helpful but not required.

steps.objective: Define an MDP, return, value function and policy; implement tabular Q-learning on a gridworld; and contrast model-free with model-based learning in sample efficiency.
steps.why: Everything on this path is a way to choose actions in an MDP; start with the problem and the simplest solver.

steps.objective: Explain how a learned world model lets an agent train a policy on imagined trajectories, and name two ways model error can be exploited by the policy.
steps.why: The atlas edge: world models support policy training through imagined trajectories.

steps.objective: Plan with a learned dynamics model in a receding-horizon loop (e.g. random shooting or CEM), executing only the first action and replanning each step.
steps.why: The atlas edge (a construction proposal, not an established result): use calibrated action-conditioned learned dynamics within receding-horizon planning, with explicit uncertainty.

steps.objective: Formulate a constrained MDP (maximize return subject to expected cost ≤ d) and explain how a safety filter differs from adding a penalty to the reward.
steps.why: The atlas edge: a predictive safety filter can modify a learner's proposed input and fall back to a previously certified plan.

steps.objective: Write the control barrier function condition ḣ(x, u) ≥ −α(h(x)) for safe set {h ≥ 0}, and implement a one-constraint QP that minimally modifies a nominal action to satisfy it.
steps.why: The atlas edge: CBF action filtering enforces a specified feasible invariance inequality, not arbitrary semantic preferences.

steps.objective: Verify stability of a continuous-time linear system ẋ = Ax by finding P ≻ 0 with AᵀP + PA ≺ 0, and explain how a CLF-CBF QP combines stability and safety and which one it relaxes when they conflict.
steps.why: The atlas edge: CLF-CBF optimization distinguishes stability and safety constraints and may relax the stability objective.

paths.title: Generative models: flows, diffusion and Schrödinger bridges
paths.summary: View generative modeling as transporting noise to data along a learned vector field: neural ODEs, flow matching, diffusion, the score-SDE unification, and endpoint-constrained bridges.
paths.audience: Learners who have trained neural networks and are comfortable with Gaussians and basic ODEs.

steps.objective: Integrate a learned vector field f_θ(x, t) from t = 0 to 1 and state the instantaneous change-of-variables formula d log p/dt = −tr(∂f/∂x) used by continuous normalizing flows.
steps.why: Every model on this path generates by integrating (or simulating) a learned field; neural ODEs are the deterministic base case.

steps.objective: Train a flow-matching model on 2-D data using the linear interpolation path xₜ = (1−t)x₀ + t x₁ and regression target x₁ − x₀, then sample by ODE integration.
steps.why: The atlas edge: continuous normalizing flows learn vector fields along probability paths and integrate them for generation; flow matching trains that field by simulation-free regression.

steps.objective: Implement the DDPM forward noising process and the noise-prediction training loss, and sample with the reverse process on a toy dataset.
steps.why: The atlas edge: flow matching admits diffusion probability paths as specific choices, and also non-diffusion paths. Diffusion is one particular path.

steps.objective: Write the reverse-time SDE dx = [f − g² ∇ₓ log pₜ(x)] dt + g dw̄ and the probability-flow ODE that shares its marginals, and relate the denoiser to the score ∇ₓ log pₜ.
steps.why: The atlas edge: the SDE framework unifies score-based and diffusion generative modeling, and its probability-flow ODE brings you back to the neural-ODE view of step 1.

steps.objective: State the Schrödinger bridge problem (the path measure closest in KL to a reference diffusion with both endpoint marginals fixed), its link to entropy-regularized optimal transport, and how iterative proportional fitting solves it.
steps.why: The atlas edge: diffusion Schrödinger bridges extend score-based generation through endpoint-constrained transport — map between two arbitrary distributions, not only noise to data.

paths.title: How deep nets learn: from kernels to developmental stages
paths.summary: Learning-dynamics theory from tractable limits (NTK, deep linear networks) to training as a control problem, singular learning theory, the local learning coefficient, and measured developmental stages and interventions.
paths.audience: Learners with solid linear algebra and probability who have trained networks and want the theory of how training unfolds.

steps.objective: Compute a GP posterior and explain how the kernel encodes the prior over functions.
steps.why: Kernel regression is the solvable reference point for the first theory of wide networks.

steps.objective: Explain why, in the NTK limit, the network output evolves as kernel gradient descent with a fixed tangent kernel, and why this lazy regime does not learn features.
steps.why: The atlas edge: infinite-width initialization connects neural networks to GPs, while training uses a tangent kernel.

steps.objective: Reproduce Saxe et al.'s result that a two-layer linear network learns the singular modes of the input–output correlation one at a time, with sigmoidal trajectories and learning time inversely proportional to singular value.
steps.why: The atlas edge: both provide tractable learning-dynamics descriptions, but their limits and parameterizations differ — deep linear nets show stagewise, feature-like learning that the NTK limit misses.

steps.objective: Frame training as a controlled dynamical system: parameters are the state, data and hyperparameters are inputs, and evaluations are outputs; give one intervention (e.g. data reweighting) and the response you would measure.
steps.why: The atlas edge: deep linear models admit explicit learning-dynamics analysis despite nonlinear parameter dynamics — the solvable case motivates treating general training as a system to predict and steer.

steps.objective: Explain why neural networks are singular models (non-identifiable, degenerate Fisher information), and state Watanabe's free-energy asymptotic F ≈ n·Lₙ + λ log n with the learning coefficient λ replacing d/2.
steps.why: The atlas edge (conditional theory): connects learning geometry to SGD using specialized local assumptions; general Adam dynamics are not covered.

steps.objective: Describe how the local learning coefficient is estimated with localized, tempered SGLD around a trained parameter, and list two settings in which the estimate is unreliable.
steps.why: The atlas edge: the LLC localizes singular statistical complexity and estimates it with tempered local sampling.

steps.objective: Summarize the evidence that changes in estimated LLC align with distinct training stages in small transformers (e.g. a transient ridge-like phase on in-context regression), and state why this is association, not causation.
steps.why: The atlas edge (empirical): changes in measured degeneracy associate with training stages in the tested models; suggestive, not universal.

steps.objective: Explain how susceptibility-guided data reweighting is used to steer which solution a model learns, and describe how the parentheses-balancing experiment uses LLC-style observables to choose and check the intervention.
steps.why: The atlas edge (measured intervention): data reweighting changes learned solution selection, extending developmental work beyond observation.

paths.title: Building capable systems: LLMs to VLAs in the closed loop
paths.summary: Climb the capability stack from transformers to language, vision-language and vision-language-action models, then place the learned policy back inside a feedback loop with a plant, sensors and actuators.
paths.audience: Learners who have trained neural networks and want a map of modern foundation-model systems and how they meet control.

steps.objective: Implement a transformer block (attention, MLP, residuals, layer norm) and explain what a causal mask does.
steps.why: The transformer is the shared backbone of every model on this path.

steps.objective: Describe the stages of an LLM pipeline — next-token pretraining, instruction tuning, preference training, and RL on verifiable outcomes — and what each stage is evaluated on.
steps.why: The atlas edge: the original transformer provides an attention-based sequence architecture; instruction training and reasoning RL are added on top.

steps.objective: Explain the LLaVA recipe: a pretrained vision encoder, a learned projection into the LLM's token space, and visual instruction tuning.
steps.why: The atlas edge: LLaVA connects a vision encoder with a language model using visual instruction tuning.

steps.objective: Contrast RT-2 (robot actions emitted as discrete tokens by a co-fine-tuned VLM) with π₀ (a VLM plus a continuous flow-matching action expert).
steps.why: The atlas edge: RT-2 co-fine-tunes visual-language models on robot-action and web data — a VLA is a VLM that outputs actions.

steps.objective: Explain diffusion policy: denoising a chunk of future actions conditioned on observations, executed in receding-horizon fashion, and why it handles multimodal demonstrations.
steps.why: The atlas edge: diffusion policy is another construction for observation-conditioned action chunks and receding-horizon execution.

steps.objective: Draw the closed loop for a VLA-driven robot (controller, actuators, plant, sensors, disturbances, fallback), identify where policy inference latency enters as a delay, and name one failure that a network-only benchmark would miss.
steps.why: The atlas edge: receding-horizon execution links action generation to closed-loop feedback; latency remains a limitation. Capability claims have to be made at the closed-loop boundary, not only for the network.

paths.title: Capstone: learning geometry meets system control
paths.summary: Walk the exact bridges from input/output data to Hankel singular values, Gramians and Fisher information, and arrive at the local learning coefficient — learning where these objects connect and where they do not.
paths.audience: Advanced learners who have done the estimation-to-control path or a linear-systems course and want the cross-cutting synthesis behind the atlas.

steps.objective: Design an input/output experiment (e.g. a step or PRBS input) for an unknown linear plant and fit an ARX model by least squares.
steps.why: Everything on this path starts from measured input/output behavior rather than assumed internal structure.

steps.objective: Run the Eigensystem Realization Algorithm on impulse-response (Markov parameter) data to obtain a reduced state-space model (A, B, C).
steps.why: The atlas edge: ERA identifies reduced linear dynamical models from response data.

steps.objective: Assemble the block Hankel matrix of Markov parameters CAᵏB, compute its SVD, and use the singular-value decay to choose a model order.
steps.why: The atlas edge: response Markov parameters populate the Hankel matrix used in ERA's SVD.

steps.objective: Perform balanced truncation on a stable LTI system and check the H∞ error bound ‖G − Gᵣ‖∞ ≤ 2 Σ (discarded Hankel singular values).
steps.why: The atlas edge: balanced truncation retains directions associated with larger Hankel singular values.

steps.objective: Explain how balanced POD builds approximate balancing modes from direct and adjoint simulation snapshots, avoiding full Gramian computation for large systems.
steps.why: The atlas edge: balanced POD uses direct and adjoint response snapshots for a scalable balancing approximation.

steps.objective: Compute reachability and observability Gramians from the Lyapunov equations A·Wc + Wc·Aᵀ + BBᵀ = 0 and Aᵀ·Wo + Wo·A + CᵀC = 0 for a stable continuous-time system, and verify σᵢ = √λᵢ(Wc·Wo).
steps.why: The atlas edge is exact: for the specified snapshot factors, the cross-snapshot SVD yields the balancing bases and Hankel singular values — the snapshots are factors of the Gramians.

steps.objective: Use the observability Gramian to rank which initial-state directions are hardest to recover from outputs.
steps.why: The atlas edge is exact: the stable LTI observability Gramian is positive definite exactly when the realization is observable.

steps.objective: Show that under known linear dynamics and independent Gaussian sensor noise, the Fisher information about the initial state equals the noise-weighted observability Gramian.
steps.why: The atlas edge is a conditional identity: this is the restricted, exact bridge from system theory to statistics.

steps.objective: Show that a regular, identifiable d-parameter model has LLC d/2, and give one reason Hankel singular values and the LLC cannot be the same quantity in general.
steps.why: The atlas edge: a locally regular identifiable model has LLC d/2, but singular loss geometry requires more than the Hessian — and the atlas marks the Hankel–LLC link as a non-equivalence.

paths.title: Capstone: capable, correctable belief-state systems
paths.summary: Connect reward misspecification, preference learning, assistance games and belief-state world models into the atlas's alignment thesis, including what would falsify it.
paths.audience: Advanced learners who know RL and the basics of LLM post-training and want the alignment synthesis behind the atlas.

steps.objective: State the RL objective as expected discounted return under a given reward, and identify where the reward comes from in a deployed system.
steps.why: Every alignment question on this path starts from what the agent is optimizing.

steps.objective: Give a concrete example where optimizing a proxy reward lowers true return, and state the scope of Skalse et al.'s result (finite MDPs, specified policy sets).
steps.why: The atlas edge: improved proxy return need not imply improved true return; the theorem is scoped to finite MDPs and policy sets.

steps.objective: Write the Bradley–Terry preference likelihood used for reward modeling, and contrast RLHF (reward model plus KL-regularized RL) with DPO (direct optimization on preference pairs).
steps.why: The atlas edge: the reward-hacking analysis studies ordering reversals between proxy and true returns — learned preference rewards are exactly such proxies.

steps.objective: Describe the cooperative inverse RL game: the robot does not know the human's reward parameter and must infer it from behavior while acting.
steps.why: The atlas edge: CIRL keeps uncertainty about a human reward parameter and models communicative teaching and learning, instead of fixing a learned reward.

steps.objective: Explain how the assistance game reduces to a coordination POMDP whose hidden state includes the human's objective, so the agent plans over a belief about it.
steps.why: The atlas edge: CIRL reduces optimal joint-policy computation to a coordination POMDP under the formal game's assumptions.

steps.objective: Explain how a learned latent world model approximates belief-state planning, and what intervention test distinguishes a valid consequence model from a good one-step predictor.
steps.why: The atlas edge: PlaNet formulates control from pixels as partial-observation planning in a learned latent model.

steps.objective: State the thesis's components (preserved measurements, explicit beliefs, action-conditioned world models, uncertainty over objectives, measured learning response) and its stated falsifier.
steps.why: The atlas edge (a thesis component, explicitly a hypothesis): learn useful action-conditioned consequence models and test their intervention validity. The thesis is rejected if better proxy optimization systematically destroys independently evaluated user utility.
